analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate tax and makes the gift tax rules permanent.
analysis.headline: The estate tax repeal bill died in the Senate Finance Committee without ever coming up for a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would eliminate the federal estate tax, which is levied on inherited wealth passing to heirs, and also eliminate a related tax on transfers that skip a generation. It would permanently set a $5 million lifetime gift tax exemption, adjusted for inflation. The bill was introduced by Sen. John Thune with 38 Republican cosponsors and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it received no further action before that Congress ended [S2][S4][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest estates — roughly those worth more than about $5 million per person at 2013 exemption levels — would pay no federal tax on inherited wealth. Very wealthy households would also gain permanent freedom to give large lifetime gifts tax-free, and the estate planning industry would keep its role serving large fortunes.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals both the estate tax and the generation-skipping transfer tax for all deaths and transfers on or after enactment [S3].

It makes permanent the maximum 35% gift tax rate and a $5 million lifetime gift tax exemption, with an inflation adjustment, so wealthy families can pass on large amounts during life without estate tax either [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would permanently lose the revenue the estate tax raises — revenue that currently comes almost entirely from the largest estates — shifting the burden to other taxpayers or other spending. Family farms and small businesses are the traditional stated concern, but only estates above the exemption threshold ever face the tax.

drawbacks.text: Repealing a tax paid almost exclusively by the largest estates would force replacement revenue from other taxpayers or add to deficits; the CRS summary does not include a revenue score, but the estate tax applies only above the exemption amount, so few estates pay it at all [S2][S3].
The bill would permanently lock in a $5 million tax-free gift channel, letting very large fortunes move between generations with no federal tax on either the gift or the eventual inheritance [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concentrated: families with estates large enough to actually owe the tax, and the professionals who advise them, would gain the most. The cost is diffuse — lost federal revenue that ordinary taxpayers and public programs must eventually absorb. Because the tax already exempts estates up to roughly $5 million per person, repeal is overwhelmingly a tax cut for the top of the wealth distribution rather than broad relief.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. John Thune introduced the bill on June 19, 2013, joined by 38 Republican cosponsors [S1][S4].
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which is where the action history ends [S5].
No markup, hearing, vote, or floor action appears in the record before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The estate tax stayed on the books, so large estates continued to owe it; the bill's sponsors and the families it targeted gained nothing, while general taxpayers were spared the lost revenue.

for.name: Sen. John Thune
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led the repeal effort.

for.name: 38 of 45 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it no Democratic cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Sen. Max Baucus (D-MT)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred; no markup or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: All 38 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and the Democratic-controlled committee never acted on it [S4][S5].

industries.note: Repeal would eliminate the only federal tax on very large inheritances, and the bill's permanent $5 million gift exemption would let fortunes move tax-free during life as well. Because the tax applies only above the exemption, the gain goes overwhelmingly to the wealthiest families while the lost revenue comes out of everyone's shared budget.

These are the traditional stated beneficiaries of estate tax repeal, since heirs sometimes face liquidity pressure paying the tax on illiquid assets. However, only estates exceeding the roughly $5 million exemption actually owe the tax, so the relief is concentrated among the largest such operations.

industries.industry: Estate planning and wealth management services
industries.note: Permanent, inflation-indexed gift and estate exemptions preserve a large continuing business in planning around and sheltering large transfers. Keeping any form of the tax keeps wealthy clients paying advisors to minimize it.
